evidence: createProject, createUser and createTask build domain objects with their constructors and save them through repository interfaces. This is application orchestration.
markTaskDone gets the task, calls the domain behavior task.markDone() and saves the result. The state-change rule stays in the domain.

requireProject and the assignee check in createTask check that referenced entities exist through repository lookups. This is a use-case precondition that needs repositories, so it belongs to the application layer.
The CreateProjectDto, CreateUserDto and CreateTaskDto interfaces are plain input contracts with no HTTP or serialization details.
The file has no storage implementation, HTTP or framework handling, or rendering code. The class doc comment says it leaves storage details to repository interfaces.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: TaskService does the work an application layer should do. It orchestrates use cases: it creates aggregates through domain constructors, checks that referenced entities exist, and saves through repository interfaces from the domain. It hands the actual state change to the domain (task.markDone()). It has no persistence code, such as SQL, file I/O or ORM calls. It has no transport or framework code, such as HTTP request or response handling, routing or status codes. It also carries no business rules that belong in domain entities. Checking that an assignee exists needs repository access, so it fits the application layer, even though it throws a DomainError. The DTO interfaces are application-level input contracts. No file in the unit carries a responsibility from another layer.
